content:
Quick answer: Joint protection means doing everyday tasks in ways that put less strain on painful joints. Use larger, stronger joints instead of small ones, spread loads, avoid tight or prolonged grips, change position often, pace activities and use gadgets such as jar openers. It works best alongside regular exercise, and an occupational therapist can tailor advice.

What joint protection is, and what it is not

Joint protection is about working smarter, not doing less. The idea is to reduce unnecessary strain on painful or inflamed joints so you can keep doing the things that matter to you with less pain and fatigue. It is widely taught by occupational therapists (OTs) and is recommended alongside exercise and other treatments for both inflammatory arthritis and osteoarthritis.

It is not about avoiding movement. Joints and muscles need regular activity to stay healthy. The aim is to balance activity and rest, use your body efficiently, and keep strength up so joints are better supported. See our exercise guide for the activity side.

Five core principles

  1. Respect pain. Pain that lasts more than an hour or two after an activity, or is worse the next day, suggests you did too much or did it in a way that strained your joints. Adjust next time rather than pushing through.
  2. Use larger, stronger joints. Carry a bag over your forearm or shoulder instead of gripping handles with your fingers. Push doors open with your shoulder or hip rather than your hand. Close drawers with your hip.
  3. Spread the load. Use both hands to lift a mug or pan. Slide heavy objects along a work surface instead of lifting them. Hold items close to your body, where they feel lighter.
  4. Avoid tight grips and staying in one position. Tight, sustained gripping, such as wringing cloths or holding a pen for a long time, stresses finger joints. Build up handles, change position often and take micro-breaks.
  5. Plan and pace. Spread heavy jobs across the week, alternate hard and easy tasks, and build in rest before you are exhausted. Our guide to energy management and pacing goes into detail.

In the kitchen

  • Use a kettle tipper, or fill the kettle with a jug, so you do not lift a full kettle.
  • Choose lightweight pans with two handles, and use a slotted spoon or a frying basket instead of draining heavy pans.
  • Try a jar opener, electric tin opener and ring-pull opener.
  • Use a perching stool so you can sit to prepare food.
  • Keep everyday items between waist and shoulder height to reduce bending and stretching.
  • Use chunky-handled or angled cutlery and knives, and a spiked chopping board to hold food steady.
  • Buy pre-chopped vegetables or frozen options on bad days. This is sensible planning, not giving up.

Around the house

  • Use long-handled dustpans, mops and grabbers to reduce bending.
  • Choose lever taps and lever door handles, or add tap turners.
  • Carry laundry in smaller loads, or use a trolley. Raise the washing basket onto a chair so you do not bend to the floor.
  • Sit to iron, or choose clothes that need little ironing.
  • Use a lightweight cordless vacuum.
  • Spread cleaning jobs over several days rather than doing everything at once.

Dressing and personal care

  • Sit down to dress, especially for socks, tights and shoes.
  • Try a long-handled shoehorn, sock aid and elastic laces.
  • Choose front-fastening clothes, larger buttons or magnetic fastenings, and zip pulls.
  • Use a toothbrush or hairbrush with a thicker handle, or add foam tubing.
  • Consider an electric toothbrush and pump-action dispensers.

Shopping, work and getting about

  • Use a shopping trolley on wheels, or shop online for heavy items.
  • Ask for bags to be packed lightly.
  • At work, set up your desk so your wrists are straight and your screen is at eye level. Use voice dictation if typing is painful. Our guide to working with arthritis covers reasonable adjustments.
  • In the car, a key turner, cushion and swivel seat can help. See our travel guide.

Gardening and hobbies

  • Use kneelers with handles, long-handled and lightweight tools, and ratchet pruners.
  • Raised beds and containers cut down on bending.
  • Work in short spells and switch between tasks.
  • For crafts, use padded or built-up needles, pens and brushes, and take regular breaks.

Protecting your hands

Hands are often the joints most affected by daily tasks. Along with the principles above, many people find these helpful:

  • Keep hands warm in the mornings. Warm water or a heat pack can ease stiffness.
  • Do regular gentle hand exercises. See our hand exercises guide.
  • Ask about splints. Resting splints worn at night or working splints during the day can support painful wrists and thumbs.
  • Avoid pinching grips, such as carrying plates between thumb and fingers. Use a tray instead.

Getting help and equipment

An occupational therapist can assess how you manage at home and at work and suggest changes, splints and equipment. You can ask your GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team for a referral, and some areas allow self-referral. Your local council's adult social care team can also arrange a needs assessment for equipment and home adaptations. Many small gadgets are available from pharmacies and online retailers, and some are free on loan through local services. Our guide to occupational therapy for hand pain explains more.

If you are buying equipment, try it first if you can. What helps one person may not suit another.

An example of pacing through the day

Joint protection works best when it is combined with pacing. Here is one way a morning might look for someone with sore hands and knees:

  • Loosen up with a warm shower and gentle hand and knee exercises before tackling anything demanding.
  • Prepare breakfast sitting on a perching stool, using a kettle tipper and a lightweight mug held in both hands.
  • Do 20 minutes of lighter housework, then sit down for a short break with a drink.
  • Split a bigger job, such as changing the bed, into two parts with a rest in between, or share it with someone else.
  • Go for a short walk later in the morning, once stiffness has eased.

Everyone's day is different. The aim is to spread demanding tasks out, switch between different types of activity, and rest before you are exhausted rather than after.

Bathroom and stairs

  • A raised toilet seat, toilet frame or grab rails make sitting and standing easier on knees and hips.
  • A bath board, bath seat or walk-in shower reduces the strain of getting in and out of the bath.
  • Use a long-handled sponge or back brush, and a towelling robe instead of drying with a towel.
  • Fit a second stair rail so you can use both hands, and keep a basket at the top and bottom of the stairs to save extra trips.
  • Your council's adult social care team can assess whether you need equipment or adaptations, and minor adaptations costing under £1,000 are usually provided free in England after an assessment.

Lifting and carrying with less strain

  1. Plan first. Is it too heavy? Can you split the load, use a trolley or ask for help?
  2. Get close. Stand close to the object with your feet hip-width apart.
  3. Bend your knees and hips rather than stooping from the waist, as far as is comfortable for your joints.
  4. Use both hands, palms up, and hold the load close to your body.
  5. Lift smoothly, avoid twisting, and turn by moving your feet.
  6. Carry less, more often. Two lighter bags, one in each hand or a backpack, are easier on joints than one heavy bag.

Techniques by joint

JointTryReduce
Hands and wristsPalms rather than fingers to push and lift; built-up handles; two-handed holds; keep wrists straightTight, sustained or pinching grips; twisting lids and taps with fingers; wringing cloths
KneesHigher chairs and a raised toilet seat; going up stairs with the stronger leg first and down with the more painful leg first; a perching stoolKneeling without a cushion, deep squatting, low seats, carrying heavy loads on stairs
HipsFirm chairs with arms; a long-handled shoehorn and grabber; sitting to dressLow sofas, crossing your legs, very long periods of standing
Back and neckWork at waist height; change position every 20 to 30 minutes; keep screens at eye levelBending and twisting together, long periods looking down, lifting from the floor
ShouldersStore everyday items between waist and shoulder height; use a step stool rather than reaching high; push rather than pullRepeated overhead reaching, carrying heavy bags on one side
Feet and anklesSupportive, cushioned footwear; insoles if advised by a podiatrist; sitting for tasks such as ironing and food preparationStanding for long periods, walking barefoot on hard floors

Posture and positioning

Staying in one position for a long time, even a comfortable one, increases stiffness. Aim to change position at least every 30 minutes. When sitting, choose a chair that lets your feet rest flat on the floor with your hips level with or slightly above your knees. A chair with arms makes standing up easier. At night, a pillow between the knees can be more comfortable for hip or knee pain when lying on your side. Avoid resting with a pillow under the knee for long periods, as this can encourage the knee to stiffen in a bent position.

Splints, supports and walking aids

A physiotherapist, occupational therapist or hand therapist can advise whether a splint or support might help you. Common options include:

  • Thumb splints for thumb-base arthritis, which NICE notes may help people with osteoarthritis of the thumb.
  • Wrist working splints to support the wrist during tasks.
  • Resting splints worn at night for inflamed hands and wrists.
  • Walking sticks, used in the hand opposite the painful hip or knee, to reduce load on the joint. Get the height checked so your elbow is slightly bent.
  • Insoles and supportive footwear for foot and ankle arthritis.

Use supports to make tasks easier, but keep up your exercises so muscles stay strong.

Joint protection during a flare

During a flare, joints are more vulnerable and fatigue is often worse. Extra steps can help:

  • Postpone heavy or non-essential tasks, and ask for help with the rest.
  • Use your gadgets and splints more, and rest the most inflamed joints in a comfortable position.
  • Keep gentle movement going so joints do not stiffen.
  • Use convenience options such as ready-prepared food or online shopping without guilt.
  • Rebuild your normal activities gradually as the flare settles.

Is it working?

After two or three weeks of using these techniques, ask yourself: Do everyday tasks hurt less? Do I have more energy left at the end of the day? Am I doing things I had stopped doing? If not, an occupational therapist can look at what you do and suggest more specific changes. If daily tasks are becoming difficult, you may also be entitled to support such as Personal Independence Payment.

When to get medical help

  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel unwell or have a high temperature.
  • See your GP if you have new joint swelling, morning stiffness that lasts more than 30 minutes, or pain that is steadily getting worse.
  • Ask for an occupational therapy or physiotherapy referral if you are struggling with daily tasks, dropping things, or worried about falls.
  • Contact your rheumatology team if you have inflammatory arthritis and frequent flares are making daily life harder.

Frequently asked questions

Does joint protection mean I should move less?

No. Joint protection is about reducing unnecessary strain, not avoiding activity. Regular exercise remains one of the most important treatments for arthritis.

Does joint protection work for osteoarthritis as well as rheumatoid arthritis?

Yes. The principles help with many types of arthritis, particularly in the hands, knees and hips.

Where can I get arthritis gadgets?

Pharmacies, mobility shops and online retailers sell many items. Occupational therapists and council adult social care teams can advise and may provide some equipment.

How do I know if I am overdoing it?

Pain or fatigue that lasts more than an hour or two after an activity, or is worse the next day, suggests you may need to pace differently.

Can I get an occupational therapy referral on the NHS?

Yes. Ask your GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team. Some areas also allow self-referral.

Should I wear a splint all the time?

Usually not. Most splints are designed for specific tasks or for night-time. Wearing them all the time can weaken muscles. Follow the advice of the therapist who provided your splint.

Which hand should I use a walking stick in?

Usually the hand on the opposite side to your painful hip or knee. A physiotherapist can check the height and how you are using it.

Are arthritis gadgets available free?

Some equipment may be provided after an occupational therapy or council needs assessment. Many small items are inexpensive to buy, and VAT relief may apply to some equipment for people with a long-term condition.
